newsitem.title: UK: UK women pay more than men for long term care insurance.
newsitem.headline: UK women pay more than men for long term care insurance.

text.p: British women are paying up to 45 percent more than men for insurance plans to pay for care in old age because of the likelihood they will live longer, insurance premium figures collected by Reuters show.

Long-term care insurance is expected to come into its own soon because of fears that the National Health Service (NHS), traditional provider of British medical services, can no longer cope with the demands of an ageing population, analysts say.
A straw poll of insurers offering policies to pay for care in old age also shows that actuaries are unsure of their figures for this relatively new market and are setting widely varying premiums.

"The disparity is because there is very little historical information from which to build risk models. So actuaries who price these policies are using their personal experiences and hunches," said an independent analyst.
"It is unlikely that two actuaries will come up with the same premium estimates given a certain situation".
The difference in monthly premiums paid by men and women can vary by between 12 and 45 percent, while lump sum payments for women can be 23 to 43 percent higher.
Mike Whittaker, product development manager at PPP Healthcare, said women on average live longer than men and often need care when they reach their seventies and eighties.
"Statistics show that more women tend to need long-term care and they tend to need it for longer," said Whittaker.

Of the insurers surveyed, BUPA made the widest differential in monthly premiums for women in their forties. Women in that age group can pay up to 45 pct more than men. Women in their fifties and sixties can pay up to 22 pct more per month.
"The younger you are the wider is the funnel of doubt for the future," said Paul Seymour, chairman of the health and care committee at the Institute of Actuaries.
The major differences in premiums quoted by the insurance companies is a result of several factors, experts said.
"It's not just the risk of a person needing care, factors like commercial arrangements for reinsurance or underwriting are also important," one actuary said.
"They might be making different assumptions on investment yields or how much is guaranteed on the underlying fund. Expenses at different offices are also an important factor".
PPP Healthcare, one of the biggest players in the market, said they had sold 10,000 long term care policies to end-1996. They expect a 50 percent surge in sales by end-1997.
"The market is relatively small and relatively new, it's not a mature product so any gains will be magnified in percentage terms," said Whittaker at PPP Healthcare.
"Independent financial advisers have already identified that long term care is going to be one of the major growth areas in insurance products".
Demand for such products is likely to rise as the costs of care for the elderly spiral.
Estimates of the cost of a year in a nursing home now range from 17,500 stg ($28,000) to 30,000 stg. By 2000 these costs are expected to grow by three to seven percent.
Home help, which costs up to 14 stg ($20) an hour now is expected to cost cost between up to 16 stg by 2000.
